SURGICAL RELEVANCE: Postoperative intra-abdominal adhesions can be asymptomatic or cause significant morbidity and mortality. Adhesion formation after hepatectomy has not been studied extensively. In the present study, the molecular mechanisms underlying intra-abdominal adhesions after hepatectomy were investigated in a murine model and in patients. Interferon (IFN) produced by natural killer T cells is a key molecule for adhesion formation after hepatectomy in mice, acting via the reciprocal balance between plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI) 1 and tissue plasminogen activator, the pivotal factors in fibrinolytic activity. This mechanism was also involved in the regulation of adhesions in human tissue samples. Hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) strongly inhibited adhesion formation by regulating IFN- and PAI-1. These results indicate that IFN- and PAI-1 are possible therapeutic targets, and HGF could prevent postoperative adhesion formation after hepatectomy.

The idea of disease originated when an illness was identified, named correctly and given a medical cause. The concept of disease is not needed to justify medical intervention or a social commitment. One might as well call all mental illnesses diseases, and call all physical diseases problems.

The problem is that this is a generalization. All mental illnesses (and every physical "disease") begin with a thought, and all physical "diseases" begin when there is a problem with the body's systems or tissues. For example, diabetes, arthritis, diabetes insipidus, pneumonia, and the like are all problems with blood sugar levels and body tissue.

Likewise, a thought that I have that makes myself sick is not necessarily a disease, depending on if, where, how, and when the thought is happening.

If someone drinks to the point that the thought occurs and is noticed, that person develops a disease when their body suffers a physical injury.

intersectionality of MSM.

The paper uses an intersectional intersection to consider the experiences of MSM who live with HIV in Swaziland, using a survey and qualitative interviews. The two types of discrimination faced by MSM are dual stigma and discrimination. Dual discrimination is when one experiences stigma due to a combination of race, gender and their HIV status. Intersectionality is used to identify and analyse the experiences of dual stigma and discrimination, and how they compare for LGBT people, single/couples, MSM and women.

Intersectionality provides a framework for understanding the experiences of dual stigma and discrimination faced by MSM living with HIV in Swaziland and highlights how programmes and policies should consider the intersectionality of MSM. This paper focuses on the intersections of race, gender and HIV status, however, it could be useful for other intersections including sexuality, sexuality among different races and different genders, disability and HIV, mental health and HIV.

The study, described in Nature, is one of the first studies comparing two similar, naturally occurring genes in their effects on the body. Protein interaction networks can represent many important aspects of biology, ranging from structural and functional information derived from experimental data to information contained in experimental and systematic biology tools (genomics data). To understand the functional and structural complexity underlying protein interactions from the networks' structure and connectivity it is critical to have tools to make and interpret network comparisons and to understand the underlying properties that confound network comparisons (i.e., the way network elements are arranged). Here we develop an experimental and systematic workflow to identify the properties underlying network similarity and network connectivity to understand the complexity of network elements that provide information about proteins. We suggest that the way elements are arranged in network comparisons helps reveal the mechanistic basis for network structures and connectivity and to highlight topology- and functional-rich elements in the network that cannot easily be inferred simply from structural and functional information in the network. A randomized trial of diazepam in detoxifying drug users

Abstract

It is well known that benzodiazepines can exacerbate withdrawal symptoms and increase relapse in drug detoxification. This study investigated whether diazepam would be beneficial in detoxifying drug users. The study was conducted at a residential treatment center. The study was conducted in a cluster randomized design. Patients were randomly assigned to one of the three groups: diazepam group, placebo group, or no intervention group. Patients were given diazepam 300 mg/day and placebo powder or placebo oral solution for 22 days. The primary outcome was relapse within 11 days of withdrawal. The secondary outcomes were the number of patients who were able to complete the detoxification process, and the number of patients who were able to stay in the residential treatment center. The diversity of the Sahara population of the murine T. testudinum has been reported to decrease over time. This study assessed whether this decline is caused by reduced fitness of individuals due to a decrease in reproductive fitness. We used a one-generation, genome-wide, simulated population model to compare the fitness of individuals in two populations of testudinum belonging to the same species. We found that individuals from the two populations showed similar fitness values, but the fitness of individuals from the southern population declined at a faster rate than the fitness of individuals from the northern population. The fitness of individuals from the southern population has been suggested to be affected by a decrease in homing ability, which may be related to a decrease in gene pool size. These results suggest that the genetic diversity in the Sahara may have been reduced due to a decrease in reproductive success of individuals in the Sahara.

Abstract

We tested whether gravid C. sculpturatus has a reduced predation efficiency in response to increasing body mass. We found that gravid females only had a modestly reduced predation efficiency. In addition, gravid females did not show either a reduced ability to detect prey or a direct reduction in the size of their predation zone. Instead, we found that gravid females generally exhibited a low maintenance cost of reproduction, and their predation efficiency was not negatively affected by their body mass. These results suggest that the reproductive costs of gravid C. sculpturatus are likely underestimated.

Discovery of a p16-encoding gene in the Drosophila ovary in 1998, p16, was followed by subsequent human and animal studies suggesting that p16 represents a novel biomarker for Parkinson's disease. Osteochondritis dissecans patellae (OCDP) is degenerative disease of the knee proximally. It is characterized by patellofemoral pain with radiating down the thigh. This pain is worse with walking, prolonged sitting, or standing for long periods. Occurring primarily in women over age 45, OCDP is a common disease of the lower extremity affecting around 6% of the female population (Nordwall K et al. 2001). Symptoms of OCDP can be severe, even disabling. Pain can occur in the knee or hip joint. Knee instability can occur even when attempting to ambulate or stand with the affected knee. An alteration in the knee’s joint range of motion is the most common feature of the disease. The disease tends to progress slow. It is usually diagnosed by a radiographic examination
